description_full: Meritage Homes Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, designs and builds single-family attached and detached homes in the United States. The company operates through two segments: Homebuilding and Financial Services. It acquires and develops land; and constructs, markets, and sells homes for entry-level and first move-up buyers in Arizona, California, Colorado, Utah, Texas, Alabama, Florida, Georgia, Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee. The company also provides title and escrow, mortgage, insurance, title insurance, and closing/settlement services to its homebuyers. Meritage Homes Corporation was founded in 1985 and is based in Scottsdale, Arizona.

financial_summary: Meritage Homes Corporation is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $4.3B market cap.
The top line has compounded at +14% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 22% against a 10% cost of capital — a 12-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 18% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $93M in free cash flow, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.26×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.
Management returns a meaningful 9.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 2.6% of the shares.

sect: Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-12.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 385 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 10% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 22% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 41% and a beta of 1.00, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.45 vs 5y 1.00), so read it loosely.
About $53.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 63% in the 2020 crash, 46% in the 2022 bear market and 76% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $37.50 (margin of safety -78%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 38%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $19.27 to $93.60 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: EV/EBITDA 14.1 vs 11.0 and P/FCF 46.4 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 56% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 2.2% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 10.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 8 covering analysts target $69.62 on average, 4% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 22% clears the cost of capital of 9.5% by 12pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.55).
Earnings quality is a concern: a weak Piotroski score of 3/9 and cash conversion of only 0.26x.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 14.1% over 3 years and 22.0% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 15%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -28.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 0.6% of sales), a maintenance pace.
It has missed earnings estimates by 6.5% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.6%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (13 sales, net $1.6M sold).
It returns 9.7% a year to shareholders (6.9% in buybacks and 2.9% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: CEO pay is $2.4M, and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
